\section[\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം}]{\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം} (vaikunnēraṁ) — "evening," built from a verb meaning "to get late"}

\label{lesson:ML-C27-vaikunneram}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Telugu reached for Sanskrit to name the evening. Malayalam's most common word takes a completely different route — an everyday verb, not a borrowed noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\textbf{\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം}} (\textbf{vaikunnēraṁ}) — "\textbf{evening}" — is, per Wiktionary, a compound: \textbf{\ml{വൈക്}} (\emph{vaikŭ}) + \textbf{-\ml{ഉം}} (\emph{-uṁ}) + \textbf{\ml{നേരം}} (\emph{nēraṁ}, "\textbf{time}"), literally "\textbf{latening time}." \textbf{\ml{നേരം}} is itself confirmed native \textbf{Proto-Dravidian} (cognate Tamil \ta{நேரம்}), not a Sanskrit borrowing — so unlike Telugu's Sanskrit \textbf{\te{సాయంత్రం}}, this whole compound is native Dravidian, start to finish. The \textbf{\ml{വൈക്}} root plausibly connects to an everyday Malayalam verb, \textbf{\ml{വൈകുക}} (\emph{vaikuka}), confirmed "\textbf{to get late}" — though be honest that this specific link is the author's own reasonable inference, not something Wiktionary's compound entry states outright.

\begin{culture}
Here's a real tension, not smoothed over: Wiktionary's own entry lists \textbf{both} "afternoon" \textbf{and} "evening" as senses of this single word. But two independently-fetched phrasebook sources (ling-app.com, talkpal.ai) draw a cleaner line — \textbf{evening} is \textbf{\ml{വൈകുന്നേരം}}, while \textbf{afternoon} gets its own, separate compound built on \textbf{\ml{ഉച്ച}} (already met, Chapter 17, "noon") plus \textbf{\ml{കഴിഞ്ഞ്}} (\emph{kazhinju}, "passed, gone by"). This project's discipline is to flag genuine disagreement rather than quietly pick whichever source is more convenient — so treat the afternoon/evening boundary here as \textbf{genuinely blurry} in the dictionary sense, even though the two everyday phrasebook sources agree on a cleaner practical split.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "vaikunnēraṁ" — "evening," literally "latening time"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the everyday verb root — vaikuka, "to get late"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest tension — Wiktionary blurs afternoon/evening; phrasebooks split them cleanly{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \ml{വൈകുന്നേരം} literally mean, and what verb is it plausibly built from? (\textbf{"Latening time"} — from \textbf{\ml{വൈകുക}}, "to get late.") Do all sources agree on where "afternoon" ends and "evening" begins for this word? (\textbf{No} — Wiktionary lists it as covering both senses; phrasebook sources instead draw a clean line, treating afternoon as a separate compound.) Is \ml{വൈകുന്നേരം} a Sanskrit borrowing, like Telugu's \te{సాయంత్రం}? (\textbf{No} — it's a native Dravidian compound, built from an everyday verb and a native "time" word, \ml{നേരം}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
